title: Open source and who actually maintains it

turns.speaker: Devon
turns.text: That library had a security hole for nine years. It's in something like a third of all server software.

turns.speaker: Priya
turns.text: And it's maintained by one person in their evenings, unpaid, who's been asking for help since about twenty sixteen.

turns.speaker: Nils
turns.text: That's the pattern rather than the exception, which is the part people find hard to believe.

turns.speaker: Devon
turns.text: How does that happen? Enormous companies depend on it.

turns.speaker: Nils
turns.text: Because it's free, so it never appears on a budget line. Nobody has to justify a dependency that costs nothing.

turns.speaker: Priya
turns.text: And the maintainer gets the obligations of a supplier with none of the revenue. Bug reports, demands, abuse when something breaks.

turns.speaker: Priya
turns.text: The burnout rate is entirely predictable.

turns.speaker: Devon
turns.text: Some funds exist now, don't they.

turns.speaker: Nils
turns.text: Several, and they've helped. The amounts are small against what the dependency is worth to the companies using it.

turns.speaker: Priya
turns.text: The awkward truth is that the licences say no warranty and everyone relies on it anyway.

turns.speaker: Devon
turns.text: Which is legally clear and practically absurd.

turns.speaker: Nils
turns.text: The European rules do start putting liability on whoever ships the product rather than on the volunteer, which is the right direction.

turns.speaker: Priya
turns.text: Assuming it doesn't make people afraid to publish anything at all.

points: A widely used library had a security flaw for nine years and is maintained by one unpaid volunteer.
Nils explains this is typical, because free software never appears on a budget and requires no justification.
Maintainers carry supplier obligations without revenue, leading to predictable burnout.
Funding initiatives exist but are small relative to the value companies derive.
Licences disclaim warranty while everyone relies on the software regardless.
European rules placing liability on those shipping products rather than volunteers are welcomed, with a caution that they may deter publishing.
